title: How long is each screw on the ruler?
description: A ruler has every centimetre cut into ten equal parts, and two screws end between its whole marks. The whole centimetres are read first, and then the parts after the mark are counted as tenths. Keeko doubts the first length and adds the parts to the whole centimetres.
teaching_notes: One idea: read the whole centimetres first, and then count the parts after the mark, each part being one tenth of a centimetre. Watch for students who add the number of parts to the whole centimetres.

source: A ruler has every centimetre split into 10 equal parts. One screw ends 7 parts after the 2 cm mark and another ends 2 parts after the 3 cm mark. Write each length and say what the first one means.
video_script.why: The child has met screws that need a smaller unit but has not yet named the small part or written a length with it.
video_script.substitution: Each small part is one tenth of a centimetre, so a length is the whole centimetres first and the tenths after them.
video_script.anchor: A ruler with every centimetre cut into ten equal parts, and two screws above it
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds the seven parts to the two whole centimetres to get 2 + 7 = 9 cm, which is past the 3 cm mark where the screw does not reach, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The first screw is two and seven tenths centimetres, and the second is three and two tenths centimetres

final_answer.value: First screw 2 7/10 cm, second screw 3 2/10 cm
final_answer.spoken: two and seven tenths centimetres, and three and two tenths centimetres

maths_rules: Each centimetre is split into 10 equal parts, so one part is 1/10 cm.
First screw: 2 whole cm and 7 parts of 1/10 cm, so 2 7/10 cm.
Second screw: 3 whole cm and 2 parts of 1/10 cm, so 3 2/10 cm.
Slip: 2 + 7 = 9 cm, but the first screw ends before the 3 cm mark, so it cannot be 9 cm.
video_script.design: One idea: each small part is one tenth of a centimetre, so a length is the whole centimetres first and the tenths after them. Assumes the child can read a ruler in whole centimetres. Wrong idea: add the parts to the whole centimetres. The ruler and the two screws stay all video; the working band builds in the idea part.

<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the first screw is nine centimetres, because two plus seven is nine.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But the screw ends before the three mark, so it cannot be that long. Seven parts are only seven tenths of one centimetre, not seven whole centimetres.
